The Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) is the fundamental numerical approximation used in direct volume ray casting to compute the color and opacity of a pixel by integrating the continuous Volume Rendering Equation (VRE) along a camera ray [S1][S15, unofficial][S24].

The claim states that the Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (DVRI) is the fundamental numerical approximation used in direct volume ray casting to compute pixel color and opacity by integrating the continuous Volume Rendering Equation (VRE). Source [S24] explicitly defines the Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) as the analytical computation of light (VRE) and states that because it cannot be computed analytically in the general case, practical algorithms 'discretize the VRI' into sequential intervals. It further denotes this expression as 'discretized VRI (DVRI)' and states that 'Expression (3) represents a common theoretical framework for all surveyed volume rendering algorithms.' Source [S1] describes the 'brute-force algorithm' of direct volume ray casting (tracing rays, resampling, and compositing front-to-back) which implements this discretization. Source [S15] describes a CPU-based direct volume rendering technique that casts rays and composites results, consistent with the DVRI framework. Therefore, the evidence supports that DVRI is the fundamental numerical approximation for direct volume ray casting.

b.  **Interpolation:** Sample the volume data at $\mathbf{p}_i$ using trilinear interpolation to get the scalar value $v_i$ [S1][S24].

The claim states that sample volume data at point p_i is interpolated using trilinear interpolation to get a scalar value v_i. Source [S1] explicitly describes the 'Sample' procedure which 'returns an approximation to the color or opacity at that point by trilinearly interpolating from the eight surrounding voxels.' It further details that for each sample location along the ray, the algorithm resamples the data by 'trilinearly interpolating from the colors and opacities in the eight voxels surrounding each sample location.' Since opacity (alpha) and color (C) are the scalar values derived from the volume data in this context, and trilinear interpolation is the specified method, the evidence fully supports the claim.
